newsitem.title: USA: Clinton makes new pledge over chemical arms treaty.
newsitem.headline: Clinton makes new pledge over chemical arms treaty.

text.p: President Bill Clinton gave new assurances to critics of a treaty outlawing chemical weapons on Thursday in an effort to gain the Senate Republican votes needed to approve the pact later in the day.

The assuraces came in a letter to Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, whose position was seen as a key to swaying undecided Republicans and producing the two-thirds Senate majority needed for approval.

Lott still did not disclose how he would vote, although he praised Clinton's efforts to give iron-clad assurances the United States would be prepared to pull out of the treaty if it produced certain adverse effects.
He called that "a major and dramatic move in the right direction" that would likely influence his thinking and that of others.

Lott disclosed the letter shortly before the Senate went into a rare closed session to discuss intelligence matters relating to the Chemical Weapons Convention, which would ban development, production or use of such weapons.

Clinton has made a major personal effort and thus had heavy political capital riding on the Senate's vote on the pact, which has already been approved by more than 70 nations and will take effect April 29 with or without U.S. backing.
A series of votes on amendments to the resolution giving consent to the treaty's ratification were to be held when the Senate resumed open session.
Four of those amendments were regarded as "killers" that would bar the United States from ratifying the treaty.
Lott, who has had talks with administration officials to get assurances on the pact, called the letter unprecedented.
"And I believe it has affected my thinking. And I believe it will others. But I'm not going to make a final statement until sometime this afternoon," he told reporters.

Clinton's letter was aimed at easing concerns that treaty provisions requiring parties to provide chemical weapons defences and calling for exchanges of peaceful chemicals and technology between nations would be used by some to spread poison gas technology to so-called rogue states.
He set out three scenarios under which he, in consultation with Congress, would be prepared to withdraw from the treaty.
-if the treaty provisions were used to justfy providing chemical weapons defensive equipment to a party that would result in degrading U.S. chemical defences;
-if it was used to justify transfers that would end the ability of a group of nations known as the Australia Group to control chemical weapons proliferation;
-or if transfers were made under the pact that jeopardised U.S. security by promoting chemical weapons proliferation.

Lott said the letter still had not satisfied some major concerns, but he qualified that with his praise of Clinton's gesture and said conditions added in lengthy negotiations had taken it out of the category of being "fundamentally flawed" -- a term he has previously used.
Earlier, Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle told reporters he was increasingly optimistic the treaty would get the two-thirds majority needed for approval.
"I think we're closer today than we have ever been," Daschle said.
